newsitem.title: GERMANY: COURT CONVICTS STEFFI GRAF'S FATHER IN TAX CASE.
newsitem.headline: COURT CONVICTS STEFFI GRAF'S FATHER IN TAX CASE.

text.p: A German court on Friday sentenced tennis star Steffi Graf's father to a jail term of three years and nine months for evading 12 million marks ($7.4 million) in taxes on his daughter's income.

The court in the southwestern city of Mannheim convicted Peter Graf, 58, on six counts of tax evasion and attempted tax evasion. It also sentenced Joachim Eckardt, a former family tax adviser, to two and a half years for assisting in the crimes.
Investigators had also targetted the world number one player in their probe into the family finances but presiding judge Joachim Plass said there was no evidence she was involved.

"After we read all the evidence and listened to all the witnesses, we decided that no active participation by Steffi Graf can be seen," he told the court, recommending the investigations against her should be dropped.

Both men remain free pending an appeal by prosecutors. Peter Graf, dressed in a dark suit, left the courtroom surrounded by bodyguards and slipped out of the building by a back entrance without speaking to reporters.
It was not immediately clear how long he would have to spend in jail as he had already spent 15 months in investigative custody while the probe and trial were taking place.

Prisoners in Germany are normally eligible for release after serving around two-thirds of their sentence -- 30 months in Graf's case. If authorities subtract the time he has already spent behind bars, he could be in jail for around 15 months.
The jail term was stiffer than the suspended sentence demanded by Graf's lawyers but fell short of prosecutors' demands for a jail term of almost six years.
Graf's lawyers said they had not yet decided if they would appeal against the sentence.

"One of the most important things for us and for the Graf family is that the court wants prosecutors to close the files in the case of Stefanie Graf," said Graf's attorney Franz Salditt, who also thanked the court for a fair trial.
Plass said he had not imposed a higher sentence partly because tax authorities had been lax in monitoring the case.
In his judgment, Plass portrayed Peter Graf as a vulnerable figure who chanelled his huge ambition into managing his daughter's career.
"Graf did not want to delegate... he wanted to keep things in his own hands," Plass said. "He wanted to be better than renowned experts."
He focused on Graf's colourful personal history including the suicide of his mother when he was a teenager, blackmail attempts against him, a breakdown and heavy drinking.

Steffi Graf left the Australian city of Melbourne on Friday on a flight to Japan shortly after her father was convicted. She declined to answer reporters' questions, saying angrily: "Haven't you guys got enough?"
The seven-times Wimbledon champion lost in the fourth round of the Australian Open last Sunday and rested in Melbourne after suffering from an infected toe and heat exhaustion.
Prosecutors had argued that Graf and Eckardt concealed a total of 19.2 million marks ($11.7 million) of tax on Steffi Graf's earnings from German authorities between 1989 and 1993.
